---
title: "Part 1 – Credibility and open research"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/housing-one-day-open-science.html#/part-1-credibility-and-open-research){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

Part 1 asks what a claim in social science is for, why people describe the field as being in crisis, how three very large studies measured the problem, and what open research proposes as a remedy, down to the software, the archives and the registries that hold its materials. The hands-on work comes at the end and runs into the first break, so that if your machine gives trouble you miss none of the talk.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, the opening | The plan of the day, the two kinds of aim, what you will understand and what you will be able to do, and what you do not need: no installation, no git, and no GitHub or OSF account. Open the [browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd) in a tab while the facilitator talks. | 8 minutes |
| Slides, Part 1 | Follow the talk: what social science is for; false positives and forking paths; the evidence from replications and many-analysts studies; incentives and questionable research practices, which matter far more than fraud; the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset, and the estimates that they returned; and why people speak of more than one 'replication' crisis. | 20 minutes |
| Slides, the three Rs and open research | Why 'replication' names three different operations, set out as a matrix of data against analysis; repeatability and credibility, with a quick check on the matrix; and the practices of open research, from open data to registered reports. | 12 minutes |
| Slides, SCORE and Multi100 | The SCORE programme and its three studies, of reproducibility, robustness and replicability, with the results of each and the finding that the three do not travel together. Then Multi100 from the position of an analyst inside it: what an analyst received, the two tasks, and how the results were put on a common scale. | 28 minutes |
| Slides, the infrastructure | Open-source software, the toolchain, plain-text file formats and what happens when you render, the archives in which data and code are kept, the browser lab and the workspace, and what the tools cannot do. An optional run of five slides covers programming languages, editors, packages, version control and licences. | 14 minutes |
| [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-1-setup) Task 1, and the [warm-up](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#warm-up) | The setup check: wait for the R engine, run the setup cell and check that `audit` has 1,014 rows. Then the warm-up, which asks you to name the R that each of four scenarios of the case describes; one of them describes none of the three. If you have installed the workspace, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in your IDE instead. | 8 minutes, and the 30-minute break after it if you need more |

**By the end of the part** you can tell apart the three operations that go under the single word 'replication', you know where the materials of a published study are kept and under which licences, and you have R running in the browser lab with the 1,014 emails of the housing-audit data loaded.
